faq: What does this tool calculate?
The UTC offset (and its standard-time baseline) for the time zone an exact coordinate pair falls in, computed from the tz database's rules for the point.
Do I need an account?
No — coordinates in, offset out.
Can I use the result for professional work?
Yes for configuration, logging and planning — the same database your systems should use. Safety-critical scheduling deserves your stack's own confirmation as well.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — you supply the coordinates; your device is not consulted.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Zone borders move with legislation; databases vintage differently, so a freshly moved border can disagree across sources briefly.
Offset versus zone name?
The offset is one number for one date; the zone name (the Timezone Map Finder's answer) is the rulebook for every date. Systems should store the name.
Ocean points?
Maritime zones give offsets too, in Etc/GMT bands — reported as the database holds them.
Historical offsets?
Rules have histories; a point's 1950 offset can differ. Date-aware tools on this site expose the idea; archival work belongs to the database's history data.
Why not just longitude ÷ 15?
Because that computes solar geography, not civil time — Spain and China are the standing disproofs.
Offsets for planning a year ahead?
Rules project forward until a legislature acts. For far-future scheduling, note the assumption; the database updates as laws land.
Can two zones share an offset?
Happily and often — which is why systems store zone names, not offsets. Today's equal offsets diverge at the next changeover.
